rv.q: So that casting pays off spectacularly well with this brand-new tour of one of Broadway’s few recent hit musicals.
The national tour of Alicia Keys ' HELL'S KITCHEN has arrived at the Eccles Theater in Salt Lake City with swagger and soul.

Hell's Kitchen never quite finds the emotional complexity its best ideas promise. But when this cast launches into another impeccably sung Alicia Keys banger, those shortcomings become surprisingly easy to forgive.
Another village did envision this show and did a damn good job. Too bad a sound system let them all down.
At its core, “Hell’s Kitchen” understands and even celebrates the passion and pain of both sides of the parent-teen dynamic, and it is that which elevates the show to a “must-see” in my book.
Most striking about this show is the way it finds an emotional core in Keys' songs, from the biggest hits to deeper cuts, that feels authentic to the story rather than forced or gratuitous.
This was a wonderful night out at the Theater.
Every ensemble number is a joy.
This isn't only a story about a book that occasionally can't keep up with its songs.
And yet: Hell’s Kitchen is irresistible.
It is undoubtedly one of the strongest examples of what a “jukebox musical” is and what they can deliver as a piece of musical theatre.
Where the film zipped along, the musical feels more earthbound, and some of the humour — particularly in the café and Amélie’s neighbourhood — feels laboured.
Alas the sound unbalance made most of the lyrics incomprehensible.

cn.t: Critics praise the tour's powerhouse vocals and emotional resonance, though some cite sound issues affecting clarity. Keys' catalog and the performances shine in this coming-of-age story.
